docs.title: DisplayLink Direct
docs.text:
DisplayLink Direct is a software development kit (SDK) that lets applications render content directly to displays connected through DisplayLink® hardware. DisplayLink (developed by Synaptics) is a software-aware hardware protocol that encodes and transmits video over standard data buses — USB 2.0, USB 3.0 — without relying on native video pass-through such as DisplayPort Alt Mode or Thunderbolt.

Instead of pushing raw, uncompressed pixels down a native display pipeline, DisplayLink compresses frame deltas on the host and packetizes that data over USB bulk transfers to a hardware decoder chip inside the dock or dongle, which drives the attached displays.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text: Unlike a traditional DisplayLink deployment, DisplayLink Direct does not require host-side graphics drivers or compositor integration. Your application talks to the SDK through a small, C-compatible API and submits frame buffers directly to each display. This makes it a lightweight, self-contained solution that is well-suited to embedded systems, kiosks, digital signage, and any application that needs deterministic, driver-free multi-display output.

docs.title: Applications
docs.text: DisplayLink Direct is a lightweight, driver-free way to drive one or many displays over USB — without a host GPU, graphics driver, or compositor. That makes it a good fit for a wide range of applications, from embedded products to large multi-display installations.

docs.title: Digital signage
docs.text: Deliver content to information boards, menu displays, and advertising screens. DisplayLink Direct can run on small, GPU-less hosts and drive multiple screens from a single device, keeping hardware and power requirements low.

docs.title: Video walls
docs.text: Span a single image or video across a grid of displays. The SDK lets you address each display by a stable hardware identifier, submit the right region of the frame to each output, and synchronize presentation across displays for a seamless wall. See the Video Wall sample.

docs.title: Embedded and industrial systems
docs.text: Add display output to embedded products, HMIs, and industrial controllers. Embedded mode performs no dynamic memory allocation at runtime, giving predictable, deterministic resource usage suitable for constrained and long-running deployments.

docs.title: Headless and GPU-less hosts
docs.text: Because frames are encoded on the CPU and decoded by the DisplayLink device, DisplayLink Direct needs no host GPU. It can run on headless servers, single-board computers, and minimal systems that have no graphics accelerator at all.

docs.title: Kiosks and point-of-sale
docs.text: Power customer-facing and operator displays for kiosks, ticketing machines, and point-of-sale terminals — often driving a primary and secondary screen from one compact host.

docs.title: Multi-monitor productivity
docs.text: Extend a workstation beyond the number of displays its native video outputs support, driving additional monitors over standard USB connections.

docs.title: Remotely controlled displays
docs.text: Drive displays from a headless or remotely managed host, where the machine generating the content is administered over the network rather than operated locally. Because DisplayLink Direct submits frames programmatically and needs no local GPU or graphics session, it suits remote and centrally managed deployments — updating signage, dashboards, or status screens from a remote controller.

docs.title: Custom rendering pipelines
docs.text: Applications that generate frames themselves — dashboards, media players, test and measurement tools — can submit frame buffers directly to displays in a range of pixel formats, with full application-level control over what appears on each output.

docs.title: Embedded Mode
docs.text:
DisplayLink Direct can run in two modes, selected at initialization time through the SDK's configuration. The mode controls how the SDK manages memory at runtime, letting you trade flexibility for determinism depending on your target system.

Hardware support required

Embedded mode is supported only on selected DisplayLink devices based on the DL-7xxx family chipset. It is not available on other devices. For details on compatible hardware and enabling this feature, please contact Synaptics.

docs.title: Non-embedded mode (default)
docs.text:
In the default mode, the SDK allocates memory dynamically at runtime as needed. This is the most flexible option and is appropriate for general-purpose hosts such as desktops, laptops, and servers, where dynamic allocation is not a concern.

  • Simplest to use — no special hardware requirements.
  • Suitable for the majority of applications.
  • Memory usage adapts to the current workload.
  • Higher performance at high display modes (resolution and refresh rate).

docs.title: Embedded mode
docs.text:
In embedded mode, the SDK does not use dynamic memory at runtime. This gives predictable, deterministic resource usage, which is important for embedded and resource-constrained systems, long-running deployments, and environments where runtime allocation is undesirable.

  • No runtime dynamic memory allocation.
  • Predictable, deterministic memory footprint.
  • Well-suited to embedded, industrial, and safety-conscious deployments.
  • May be constrained at high display modes compared to non-embedded mode.

Firmware update not available

Automatic and manual firmware update is not available in embedded mode. Ensure the device is running compatible firmware before using embedded mode.

docs.title: Resolution limits
docs.text:
In embedded mode, the maximum supported resolution depends on how many outputs are driven:

Configuration Max width Max height Single output 5120 px 2160 px Multiple outputs 1920 px 1080 px

docs.title: Enabling embedded mode
docs.text:
Embedded mode is enabled through the SDK configuration when initializing the system. Set the embeddedMode flag in the configuration before initialization:

CC++Python 
#include <dlsdk/dlsdk.h>

dlsdk_config config = {0};
config.size = sizeof(config);
config.embeddedMode = 1;

dlsdk_initialise_with_config(&config);

#include <dlsdk/dlsdk.h>

// firmwarePath = nullptr, firmware update not supported in embedded mode
dl::sdk::Config config(nullptr, /*embeddedMode=*/true);
dl::sdk::System system(config);

import dlsdk

config = dlsdk.Config()
config.embedded_mode = True
dlsdk.create_system(config)

Note

If the connected device does not support embedded mode, enabling this flag will not have the intended effect. Ensure you are using a compatible DL-7xxx family device — contact Synaptics if you are unsure.

docs.title: C++ API Documentation
docs.text:
Info

See Minimal Example for a minimal usage example that powers on a display and presents a solid-color frame.

The C++ helper classes are declared in include/dlsdk/dlsdk.h, in the dl::sdk namespace. They are thin wrappers around the C API and are provided as example code, built directly on top of the same dlsdk_* functions documented there.

Objects are created in the following order: a dl::sdk::System is initialized first, which is then used to enumerate dl::sdk::DeviceHandle objects, which in turn expose their attached dl::sdk::DisplayHandle objects. This page documents the API in that same order: System, Device, Display, then DP AUX.

docs.title: Thread Safety
docs.text: API calls made on the same handle object (e.g. dl::sdk::DeviceHandle, dl::sdk::DisplayHandle, dl::sdk::DpAux) are generally not thread-safe. The user should avoid calling the API with the same handle concurrently from multiple threads, unless the user provides their own synchronization to serialize access to that handle.

docs.title: registerHotplugCallback()
docs.text:
dlsdk_status registerHotplugCallback(const CallbackFn& cb, CallbackHandle* outHandle);

Register a hotplug callback function.

Details: This function registers a callback to be invoked when a hotplug event occurs and returns a registration handle for later unregistration. Only one callback can be registered, and registering a new callback will overwrite the previous one. The callback will be invoked for all hotplug events from the moment the callback is registered. When a system is destroyed, all hotplug callbacks will be automatically unregistered and their handles invalidated.

Parameters: - cb — the function to be invoked when a hotplug event occurs. Must be non-NULL. - outHandle — Callback registration handle. Must be non-NULL. On success, receives a non-NULL handle.

Returns: DLSDK_SUCCESS on success, otherwise an error code.

docs.title: unregisterHotplugCallback()
docs.text:
dlsdk_status unregisterHotplugCallback(CallbackHandle handle);

Unregisters a hotplug callback.

Details: You must not register or unregister callbacks from within a callback. Callback will not be invoked after this function returns successfully. If the callback is currently running, this function will block until it completes before unregistering and returning.

Parameters: - handle — The callback registration handle returned during registration.

Returns: DLSDK_SUCCESS on success, DLSDK_INVALID_HANDLE if handle is unknown or already unregistered, otherwise an error code.

std::vector<DisplayHandle> getDisplays();

Function used to obtain the attached displays for a given device.

Details: Display handles are owned by their device and must not be freed by the caller; they remain valid until the associated device handle is released with DeviceHandle::release() or DeviceHandle::restartAndFreeDevice().

docs.title: getDpAux()
docs.text:
DpAux getDpAux(unsigned int output);

Function used to obtain a handle to the DP AUX channel available on a given device.

Details: Some devices may not have a DP AUX channel, in which case this function will return an invalid DpAux. This function is useful when low-level access to the DP AUX channel is required and display is not enumerated automatically. Otherwise, it is recommended to obtain the DP AUX channel via DisplayHandle::getDpAux().

Parameters: - output — The output index for which to obtain the DP AUX channel handle.

Returns: A DpAux object, or an invalid one if the device does not support it, output is not DP type or it does not exist.

docs.title: updateFirmware()
docs.text:
dlsdk_status updateFirmware(const char* firmwarePath);

Function used to update the firmware of a device.

Details: Synchronous function used to update the firmware on a specific device. This function will block until the firmware update process is complete, which may take up to 30seconds on the device. This method must be called by the user to update the firmware on a specific device. This is required when the SDK is initialised with null firmware path, and can be used to update the firmware on demand. It is advised to keep the firmware up to date to ensure the best performance and reliability of the device, as well as access to the latest features. After a successful firmware update, the device or display handle is still valid, but keep in mind that the rendering pipeline must be established and the display has to be powered on again.

Parameters: - firmwarePath — The path to the firmware directory provided by DisplayLink. Must be valid and non-NULL.

Returns: DLSDK_SUCCESS on success, otherwise an error code. DLSDK_UNSUCCESSFUL_NO_DEVICE if the device is not found within 15seconds after firmware update.

See Firmware Update for more on firmware-related workflows.

docs.title: show()
docs.text:
dlsdk_status show(dlsdk_pixel_format format, const void* pixels, unsigned int stride = 0);

Function to present the contents of a pixel buffer on the display.

Details: This is a non-blocking call and will return before the pixels are displayed. If the user wishes notification of when the pixels have been displayed, they should call DisplayHandle::waitOnShow()

Parameters: - format — The pixel format contained in the pixel buffer - pixels — The buffer containing the pixels to be displayed - stride — Number of bytes that needed to add to the address of the first pixel of a row in order to go to the address of the first pixel of the next row. If a value of 0 is given then it will be automatically calculated as bytes per pixel * display width

Returns: DLSDK_SUCCESS if the frame was successfully submitted for rendering, or an error code on failure. The caller should check the render and frame transmission status with DisplayHandle::waitOnShow().

docs.title: waitOnShow()
docs.text:
dlsdk_status waitOnShow(std::chrono::milliseconds timeout = std::chrono::milliseconds::max());

Function used to block for notification that pixels have been displayed after calling DisplayHandle::show(), with an optional timeout.

Parameters: - timeout — Maximum time to wait. Defaults to waiting indefinitely (std::chrono::milliseconds::max()).

Returns:

  • DLSDK_SUCCESS when the pixels have been displayed
  • DLSDK_UNSUCCESSFUL_NO_MONITOR when display is not ready
  • DLSDK_BUSY when the device aborted a previously submitted frame due to resource constraints. The caller should retry DisplayHandle::show() with the frame to be displayed, which will typically involve more aggressive compression, or proceed with new frame if the previous frame is no longer relevant.
  • DLSDK_TIMEOUT if waiting for the display to be ready timed out
  • DLSDK_UNSUCCESSFUL on unknown error

dlsdk_aux_status auxReadData(uint32_t auxRegAddress, uint8_t* data, uint8_t length);

docs.title: C API
docs.text:
The C API is declared in include/dlsdk/dlsdk.h and is the primary, ABI-stable interface exposed by DisplayLink Direct. The C++ helper classes (dl::sdk::System, dl::sdk::DeviceHandle, dl::sdk::DisplayHandle, ...) are thin wrappers around these same functions.

All functions are exported via DLSDK_EXPORT and are safe to call from C or C++ (the header wraps declarations in extern "C").

Objects are created in the following order: a System is initialized first, which is then used to enumerate Devices, which in turn expose their attached Displays. This section documents the API in that same order: System, Device, Display, then DP AUX.

docs.title: dlsdk_status status codes
docs.text:
API method status return codes.

Value Meaning DLSDK_SUCCESS The call completed successfully. DLSDK_NOT_ENOUGH_SPACE The provided output buffer is too small; reallocate using the returned required size and call again. DLSDK_UNSUCCESSFUL Generic failure. DLSDK_UNSUCCESSFUL_NO_DEVICE No device was found (e.g. after a firmware update, within the expected wait window). DLSDK_UNSUCCESSFUL_NO_MONITOR The display is not ready / no monitor detected. DLSDK_UNSUCCESSFUL_MONITOR_OFF The monitor is powered off. DLSDK_INVALID_HANDLE The provided handle is invalid or unknown. DLSDK_INVALID_ARGS One or more arguments are invalid. DLSDK_TIMEOUT The operation timed out. DLSDK_NOT_IMPLEMENTED The requested functionality is not implemented. DLSDK_BUSY The device aborted a previously submitted frame due to resource constraints; retry dlsdk_display_show().

docs.title: dlsdk_hotplug_event
docs.text: Hotplug event types: DLSDK_HOTPLUG_EVENT_DEVICE_ARRIVED, DLSDK_HOTPLUG_EVENT_DEVICE_REMOVED, DLSDK_HOTPLUG_EVENT_DISPLAY_ARRIVED, DLSDK_HOTPLUG_EVENT_DISPLAY_REMOVED.

docs.title: dlsdk_hotplug_event_data
docs.text:
Data provided to hotplug callbacks when a hotplug event occurs.

Handle validity rules:

  • On DLSDK_HOTPLUG_EVENT_DEVICE_ARRIVED, device is valid during the callback and will remain valid until a corresponding DLSDK_HOTPLUG_EVENT_DEVICE_REMOVED event is received for the same device.
  • On DLSDK_HOTPLUG_EVENT_DEVICE_REMOVED, device is informational only and must not be used with device API calls.
  • On DLSDK_HOTPLUG_EVENT_DISPLAY_ARRIVED, display is valid during the callback. Will be NULL if the event is not for a display (e.g. device hotplug event).
  • On DLSDK_HOTPLUG_EVENT_DISPLAY_REMOVED, display is informational only and must not be used with display API calls.
Field Description version Struct version set by the SDK. event The type of hotplug event that occurred. device Handle to the device on which the event occurred. device_id Unique identifier for the device involved in the event. Valid for the duration of the callback. display Handle to the display involved in the event if applicable. display_id Unique identifier for the display involved in the event. Valid for the duration of the callback.

docs.title: dlsdk_get_devices
docs.text:
dlsdk_status dlsdk_get_devices(dlsdk_device_handle* devices, unsigned int* size);

Function used to obtain the attached devices.

Details: The caller must allocate enough memory to store the device handles (dlsdk_device_handle) before calling this method. If there are more attached devices than memory allocated, the function will return DLSDK_NOT_ENOUGH_SPACE. If this happens, the user must then allocate memory equal to the value of the returned size before calling this function again.

Parameters:

  • devices — A pointer to a contiguous piece of memory big enough to store the number of connected device handles. If NULL is passed, the function will only return the number of connected devices in size parameter.
  • size — [in]: the number of device handles that can be stored in the devices parameter. [out]: The number of attached devices.

Returns: DLSDK_NOT_ENOUGH_SPACE if there are more attached devices than allocated memory for storing dlsdk_device_handle.

docs.title: dlsdk_register_hotplug_callback
docs.text:
dlsdk_status dlsdk_register_hotplug_callback(dlsdk_hotplug_callback_fn cb, void* user_data, dlsdk_hotplug_callback_handle* outHandle);

Register a hotplug callback function.

Details: This function registers a callback to be invoked when a hotplug event occurs and returns a registration handle for later unregistration. Only one callback can be registered, and registering a new callback will overwrite the previous one. The callback will be invoked for all hotplug events from the moment the callback is registered. When a system is destroyed, all hotplug callbacks will be automatically unregistered and their handles invalidated.

Parameters:

  • cb — the function to be invoked when a hotplug event occurs. Must be non-NULL.
  • user_data — user data to pass to the callback function. Can be NULL if not needed.
  • outHandle — Callback registration handle. Must be non-NULL. On success, receives a non-NULL handle.

Returns: DLSDK_SUCCESS on success, otherwise an error code.

docs.title: dlsdk_unregister_hotplug_callback
docs.text:
dlsdk_status dlsdk_unregister_hotplug_callback(dlsdk_hotplug_callback_handle handle);

Unregisters a hotplug callback.

Details: You must not register or unregister callbacks from within a callback. Callback will not be invoked after this function returns successfully. If the callback is currently running, this function will block until it completes before unregistering and returning.

Parameters:

  • handle — The callback registration handle returned during registration.

Returns: DLSDK_SUCCESS on success, DLSDK_INVALID_HANDLE if handle is unknown or already unregistered, otherwise an error code.

docs.title: dlsdk_device_id
docs.text:
const char* dlsdk_device_id(dlsdk_device_handle device);

Function used to obtain the unique identifier of the device.

Details: Based on the device's USB serial number, so the identifier persists across unplugging and power cycling. Example: "USB_6015-10096418", where 6015 is the USB product ID (in hex) and 10096418 is the serial number. The DisplayLink USB vendor ID (0x17e9) is not included.

Parameters:

  • device — Device handle. Must be valid and non-NULL

Returns: A string containing the unique device identifier.

Example:

CC++Python 
const char* id = dlsdk_device_id(device);
printf("%s\n", id); // e.g. USB_6015-10096418

std::string id = device.id();
std::cout << id << std::endl; // e.g. USB_6015-10096418

device_id = device.id()
print(device_id)  # e.g. USB_6015-10096418

docs.title: dlsdk_device_get_displays
docs.text:
dlsdk_status dlsdk_device_get_displays(dlsdk_device_handle device, dlsdk_display_handle* displays, unsigned int* size);

Function used to obtain the attached displays for a given device.

Details: The caller must allocate enough memory to store the display handles (dlsdk_display_handle) before calling this method. If there are more attached displays than memory allocated, the function will return DLSDK_NOT_ENOUGH_SPACE. If this happens, the user must then allocate memory equal to the value of the returned size before calling this function again. Display handles are owned by their device and must not be freed by the caller; they remain valid until the associated device handle is released with dlsdk_free_device(), dlsdk_restart_and_free_device() or dlsdk_teardown().

Parameters:

  • device — Device handle. Must be valid and non-NULL
  • displays — A pointer to a contiguous piece of memory big enough to store the number of display handles connected to the device. If NULL, the function will only return the number of attached displays in size parameter.
  • size — [in]: the number of display handles that can be stored in the displays parameter. [out]: The number of attached displays.

Returns: DLSDK_NOT_ENOUGH_SPACE if there are more attached displays than allocated memory for storing dlsdk_display_handle.

docs.title: dlsdk_device_get_dpaux
docs.text:
dlsdk_dpaux_handle dlsdk_device_get_dpaux(dlsdk_device_handle device, unsigned int output);

Function used to obtain a handle to the DP AUX channel available on a given device.

Details: Some devices may not have a DP AUX channel, in which case this function will return NULL. This function is useful when low-level access to the DP AUX channel is required and display is not enumerated automatically. Otherwise, it is recommended to obtain the DP AUX channel handle via the display object using dlsdk_display_get_dpaux().

Parameters:

  • device — Device handle. Must be valid and non-NULL
  • output — The output index for which to obtain the DP AUX channel handle

Returns: A handle to the DP AUX channel or NULL if the device does not support it, output is not DP type or it does not exist.

docs.title: dlsdk_device_update_firmware
docs.text:
dlsdk_status dlsdk_device_update_firmware(dlsdk_device_handle device, const char* firmwarePath);

Function used to update the firmware of a device.

Details: Synchronous function used to update the firmware on a specific device. This function will block until the firmware update process is complete, which may take up to 30seconds on the device. This method must be called by the user to update the firmware on a specific device. This is required when the SDK is initialised with null firmware path, and can be used to update the firmware on demand. It is advised to keep the firmware up to date to ensure the best performance and reliability of the device, as well as access to the latest features. After a successful firmware update, the device or display handle is still valid, but keep in mind that the rendering pipeline must be established and the display has to be powered on again.

Parameters:

  • device — The device handle. Must be valid and non-NULL.
  • firmwarePath — The path to the firmware directory provided by DisplayLink. Must be valid and non-NULL.

Returns: DLSDK_SUCCESS on success, otherwise an error code. DLSDK_UNSUCCESSFUL_NO_DEVICE if the device is not found within 15 seconds after firmware update.

See Firmware Update for more on firmware-related workflows.

docs.text: Functions for manipulating/controlling displays attached to a device.

docs.title: dlsdk_display_id
docs.text:
const char* dlsdk_display_id(dlsdk_display_handle display);

Function used to obtain the unique identifier of the display.

Details: Identifies a single output on a device; a device with multiple outputs (e.g. up to 4 HDMI connectors) exposes one identifier per output. Example: "USB_6015-10096418^0", "USB_6015-10096418^1", "USB_6015-10096418^2", "USB_6015-10096418^3", where 6015 is the USB product ID (in hex), 10096418 is the serial number, and the suffix after ^ is the output index. The DisplayLink USB vendor ID (0x17e9) is not included.

Parameters:

  • display — Display handle. Must be valid and non-NULL

Returns: A string containing the device and head identifiers.

Example:

CC++Python 
const char* id = dlsdk_display_id(display);
printf("%s\n", id); // e.g. USB_6015-10096418^0

std::string id = display.id();
std::cout << id << std::endl; // e.g. USB_6015-10096418^0

display_id = display.id()
print(display_id)  # e.g. USB_6015-10096418^0

docs.title: dlsdk_display_show
docs.text:
dlsdk_status dlsdk_display_show(dlsdk_display_handle display, dlsdk_pixel_format format, const void* pixels, unsigned int stride);

Function to present the contents of a pixel buffer on the display.

Details: This is a non-blocking call and will return before the pixels are displayed. If the user wishes notification of when the pixels have been displayed, they should call dlsdk_display_wait_on_show()

Parameters:

  • display — Display handle. Must be valid and non-NULL
  • format — The pixel format contained in the pixel buffer
  • pixels — The buffer containing the pixels to be displayed
  • stride — Number of bytes that needed to add to the address of the first pixel of a row in order to go to the address of the first pixel of the next row. If a value of 0 is given then it will be automatically calculated as bytes per pixel * display width

Returns: DLSDK_SUCCESS if the frame was successfully submitted for rendering, or an error code on failure. The caller should check the render and frame transmission status with dlsdk_display_wait_on_show().

docs.title: dlsdk_display_wait_on_show
docs.text:
dlsdk_status dlsdk_display_wait_on_show(dlsdk_display_handle display);

Function used to block for notification that pixels have been displayed after calling dlsdk_display_show().

Parameters:

  • display — Display handle. Must be valid and non-NULL

Returns:

  • DLSDK_SUCCESS when the pixels have been displayed
  • DLSDK_UNSUCCESSFUL_NO_MONITOR when display is not ready
  • DLSDK_BUSY when the device aborted a previously submitted frame due to resource constraints. The caller should retry dlsdk_display_show() with the frame to be displayed, which will typically involve more aggressive compression, or proceed with new frame if the previous frame is no longer relevant.
  • DLSDK_TIMEOUT if waiting for the display to be ready timed out
  • DLSDK_UNSUCCESSFUL on unknown error

docs.title: DP AUX API
docs.text: Low-level access to the DisplayPort AUX channel, useful when direct AUX/I2C access is required beyond the automatic display enumeration.

docs.title: dlsdk_dpaux_read
docs.text:
dlsdk_aux_status dlsdk_dpaux_read(dlsdk_dpaux_handle dpaux, uint32_t auxRegAddress, uint8_t* data, uint8_t length);

Reads data from native DP AUX registers using 16-byte burst transactions. Larger requests are serviced by chaining multiple burst reads into the provided buffer. The function waits for a response (up to 400us).

Parameters:

  • dpaux — DP AUX channel handle. Must be valid and non-NULL
  • auxRegAddress — DP register address
  • data — Buffer for incoming data
  • length — Data buffer length (0 <= length < 256)

Returns: status response from DP peer

  • auxRegAddress — DP register address

docs.title: Python API Documentation
docs.text:
Info

See Minimal Example for a minimal usage example that powers on a display and presents a solid-color frame.

The Python bindings are a thin pybind11 wrapper around the same C API declared in include/dlsdk/dlsdk.h, exposed as the dlsdk module.

Objects are created in the following order: the module-level system functions are called first, which are then used to enumerate dlsdk.Device objects, which in turn expose their attached dlsdk.Display objects. This page documents the API in that same order: System, Device, Display, then DP AUX.

docs.title: Thread Safety
docs.text: API calls made on the same object (e.g. dlsdk.Device, dlsdk.Display, dlsdk.DpAux) are generally not thread-safe. The user should avoid calling the API with the same object concurrently from multiple threads, unless the user provides their own synchronization to serialize access to that object.

docs.title: Minimal Usage Example
docs.text:
Power on the first display of the first attached device and fill it with brand blue (#0081c6), assuming exactly one device and one display are connected.

CC++Python 
#include <dlsdk/dlsdk.h>
#include <assert.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <unistd.h>

int main(void)
{
  dlsdk_initialise();

  dlsdk_device_handle device;
  unsigned int device_count = 1;
  assert(dlsdk_get_devices(&device, &device_count) == DLSDK_SUCCESS && device_count == 1); /* exactly one device connected */

  dlsdk_display_handle display;
  unsigned int display_count = 1;
  assert(dlsdk_device_get_displays(device, &display, &display_count) == DLSDK_SUCCESS && display_count == 1); /* exactly one display connected */

  dlsdk_display_power_on(display);

  struct dlsdk_rect size = dlsdk_display_size(display);
  uint32_t* pixels = (uint32_t*)malloc((size_t)size.width * size.height * sizeof(uint32_t));
  for (unsigned int i = 0; i < size.width * size.height; ++i) {
    pixels[i] = 0xFF0081C6; /* brand blue #0081c6, DLSDK_PIXEL_FORMAT_XRGB byte order is B,G,R,X */
  }

  dlsdk_display_show(display, DLSDK_PIXEL_FORMAT_XRGB, pixels, 0);
  dlsdk_display_wait_on_show(display);

  sleep(10); /* keep the frame visible for 10 seconds */

  free(pixels);
  dlsdk_free_device(device);
  dlsdk_teardown();
  return 0;
}

#include <dlsdk/dlsdk.h>
#include <cassert>
#include <chrono>
#include <cstdint>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

int main()
{
  dl::sdk::System system;

  std::vector<dl::sdk::DeviceHandle> devices = system.getDevices();
  assert(devices.size() == 1); // exactly one device connected
  dl::sdk::DeviceHandle& device = devices.front();

  std::vector<dl::sdk::DisplayHandle> displays = device.getDisplays();
  assert(displays.size() == 1); // exactly one display connected
  dl::sdk::DisplayHandle& display = displays.front();

  display.powerOn();

  dl::sdk::Rect size = display.size();
  std::vector<uint32_t> pixels(size.width * size.height, 0xFF0081C6); // brand blue #0081c6, DLSDK_PIXEL_FORMAT_XRGB byte order is B,G,R,X

  display.show(DLSDK_PIXEL_FORMAT_XRGB, pixels.data());
  display.waitOnShow();

  std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::seconds(10)); // keep the frame visible for 10 seconds

  return 0;
}

import time

import numpy as np
import dlsdk

dlsdk.create_system()

devices = dlsdk.get_devices()
assert len(devices) == 1  # exactly one device connected
device = devices[0]

displays = device.get_displays()
assert len(displays) == 1  # exactly one display connected
display = displays[0]
display.power_on()

size = display.size()
frame = np.empty((size.height, size.width, 4), dtype=np.uint8)
frame[:, :, 0] = 0xC6  # B
frame[:, :, 1] = 0x81  # G
frame[:, :, 2] = 0x00  # R
frame[:, :, 3] = 0xFF  # X (unused), DLSDK_PIXEL_FORMAT_XRGB byte order is B,G,R,X

display.show(dlsdk.DLSDK_PIXEL_FORMAT_XRGB, frame)
display.wait_on_show()

time.sleep(10)  # keep the frame visible for 10 seconds

dlsdk.delete_system()

docs.title: Qt Platform Plugin
docs.text:
How to use the DisplayLink Direct Qt platform plugin to render Qt applications to DisplayLink displays.

The qdlsdk plugin is a Qt Platform Abstraction (QPA) plugin that lets an unmodified Qt GUI application render directly onto DisplayLink Direct displays, without requiring a Linux graphical environment such as X11, Wayland, GNOME, or any other compositor. Qt applications can run directly from a virtual terminal (VT) without a GPU. It registers itself under the platform name dlsdk and is selected the same way as any other QPA plugin, via the -platform command-line argument or the QT_QPA_PLATFORM environment variable.

Distributed separately

The Qt platform plugin is built and distributed from its own repository, separate from the core DisplayLink Direct SDK described elsewhere in this documentation. It links against the dlsdk::dlsdk CMake target described in Running on Linux.

Source repository: syna-isd/displaylink-dlsdk-qt.

docs.title: Input handling
docs.text:
Input handling is Qt's responsibility, not DisplayLink Direct's: the plugin does not read input from DisplayLink devices or hardware in any way. It simply wires up Qt's existing standard Linux input backends, the same way other Linux QPA plugins (e.g. eglfs, linuxfb) do:

  • libinput is used when Qt was built with libinput support.
  • Otherwise the plugin falls back to evdev keyboard, mouse and touch managers.

docs.title: Running an application
docs.text:
Point QT_PLUGIN_PATH at the plugin's plugins output directory and pass -platform dlsdk to your application:

QT_PLUGIN_PATH=/path/to/build/src/plugin/plugins ./my-qt-app -platform dlsdk

USB permissions

Accessing DisplayLink USB devices requires the same permissions described in USB permissions. Without them, the plugin may need to be run with sudo, or the running user added to a group with access to /dev/bus/usb/*.

docs.text:
The PyDisplayLinkScreensaver sample demonstrates how to use the DisplayLink Direct Python bindings to render animated content on a connected display. The app uses pygame to render a bouncing DisplayLink logo and streams each frame to the device using the DisplayLink Direct Python module.

This sample is useful for validating end-to-end Python rendering performance, checking display connectivity, and learning how to push RGB frame buffers from Python.

  • Python 3.10+

docs.text:
Create a virtual environment and install dependencies:

cd samples/PyDisplayLinkScreensaver
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

Run the sample:

python pylogo.py

docs.text:

  • Asserts exactly one connected device and one connected display
  • Powers on the display and queries display resolution
  • Renders a bouncing DisplayLink logo on a white background

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Read EDID sample demonstrates how to use the DisplayLink Direct API to read and retrieve Extended Display Identification Data (EDID) from connected DisplayLink displays. EDID is crucial information stored in every monitor that identifies the display's vendor, model, supported resolutions, refresh rates, color capabilities, and other display characteristics. This sample shows how to access this data using the DP AUX (DisplayPort Auxiliary) channel, which is used to read display capabilities and configuration.

Chip Family Compatibility

This sample is only compatible with DL-7xxx chip family DisplayLink devices.

docs.title: EDID Details
docs.text:
EDID (Extended Display Identification Data) is a standard that contains: - Vendor ID and product information - Supported display resolutions and refresh rates - Color depth capabilities - Timing information and video modes - Display connector type - Serial number and model name

This information helps applications and systems understand what a display can do and configure themselves accordingly.

docs.title: Source Code
docs.text: The complete implementation of the Read EDID sample is available in samples/dl-get-edid.cpp.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• DisplayLink Direct SDK installed
  • CMake 3.10 or higher
  • C++17 compatible compiler

docs.title: Build Instructions
docs.text:
Navigate to the samples directory and build using CMake:

cd samples
cmake -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/path/to/dlsdk -S . -B build
cmake --build build

docs.title: Running the Application
docs.text:
Run the dl-get-edid application to read EDID data:

# Read EDID from the first device, first output
./dl-get-edid

# Read EDID from a specific device and output
./dl-get-edid -d 0 -o 0

# Read EDID with quiet mode (no status messages)
./dl-get-edid -d 1 -o 2 -q

# Display help information
./dl-get-edid -h

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• -d \<device>: Device number to query (default: 0). Use 0 to (device count - 1)
  • -o \<output>: Output/display number on the device (default: 0). Use 0 to (output count - 1)
  • -q: Quiet mode - suppresses status messages, useful for scripting
  • -h: Display help message

docs.title: Output
docs.text: The application prints the raw EDID binary data to standard output. The EDID data is typically 128 bytes (or 256 bytes for extended EDID) and can be: - Redirected to a file for analysis - Parsed by external tools to extract display information - Used for system configuration scripts

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• All connected monitors must be powered on to read their EDID
  • Use Ctrl+C to exit the application
  • For parsing and analyzing EDID data, various online tools and specifications are available
  • On Ubuntu systems, you can install and use the read-edid package to decode the EDID data: 
    sudo apt-get install read-edid
./dl-get-edid | edid-decode

display_wait_on_show()

When using multiple displays, call show on each display followed by wait_on_show on each display to help synchronise outputs

docs.title: Identifying devices and displays
docs.text:
The hardware ID functions can be used to identify a particular device or display so the right image can be sent.

device_id uses the USB serial number which is programmed into the hardware and remains the same after unplugging or power cycling

Example

USB_6015-10096418

display_id identifies a particular output on a hardware device. For example a device may have up to 4 HDMI output connectors.

Example

USB_6015-10096418^0

If the driver needs to be installed manually, visit:

For Linux, download linux.zip from the release assets and unzip it into the libs/ directory of your checkout.

docs.title: Firmware Update
docs.text: For proper operation, the DisplayLink device firmware must be kept up to date. DisplayLink Direct is validated against the firmware versions listed in the release notes for each release.

docs.title: Firmware packages
docs.text:
Firmware is distributed as pre-built binary packages (.spkg files) via GitHub Release Assets. Download the firmware package firmware.zip from the release assets and unpack it into the DL-firmware/ directory of your checkout.

Each .spkg file targets a specific DisplayLink device family, for example:

  • ella-dock-release.spkg for DL-3xxx
  • firefly-monitor-release.spkg for DL-4xxx
  • ridge-dock-release.spkg for DL-6xxx
  • navarro-dock-release.spkg for DL-7xxx

docs.title: Supported firmware versions
docs.text:
The firmware versions bundled with the current release published in the release notes.

Firmware compatibility

Older DisplayLink Direct releases may be incompatible with devices running newer firmware. In that case, the device may not be enumerated by the SDK at all.

When a device is running outdated firmware, the device may still enumerate, but available capabilities may be reduced or behave differently until the firmware is updated.

docs.title: Read firmware version
docs.text:
Use the device handle to query the firmware version currently running on the device.

CC++Python 
#include <stdio.h>
#include <dlsdk/dlsdk.h>

dlsdk_initialise();

dlsdk_device_handle devices[4];
unsigned int count = 4;
if (dlsdk_get_devices(devices, &count) == DLSDK_SUCCESS && count > 0) {
    for (unsigned int i = 0; i < count; ++i) {
        const char* version = dlsdk_device_firmware_version(devices[i]);
        printf("Device %u firmware version: %s\n", i, version ? version : "unknown");
    }
}

dlsdk_teardown();

#include <iostream>
#include <dlsdk/dlsdk.h>

dl::sdk::System system;
auto devices = system.getDevices();

for (std::size_t i = 0; i < devices.size(); ++i) {
    std::cout << "Device " << i
              << " firmware version: " << devices[i].firmwareVersion()
              << std::endl;
}

import dlsdk

dlsdk.create_system(dlsdk.Config())

devices = dlsdk.get_devices()
for index, device in enumerate(devices):
    print(f"Device {index} firmware version: {device.firmware_version()}")

dlsdk.delete_system()

docs.title: Update process
docs.text:
Firmware is applied by the SDK when a connected device is running a different version than the provided firmware. Ensure the DL-firmware/ directory contains the correct .spkg packages before initializing the system.

Firmware path must point to a directory

All firmware update API calls require a path to a directory containing the .spkg files, not a path to a single firmware file. During the update process, DisplayLink Direct identifies the enumerated device family and selects the matching firmware package from that directory.

There are two ways to update firmware: automatic update at initialization, or manual update on demand.

Embedded mode

Automatic and manual firmware update is not available in embedded mode. Ensure the device is running compatible firmware before using embedded mode.

To update firmware, perform the update in non-embedded mode first.

docs.title: Automatic firmware update
docs.text:
When the system is initialized with a valid firmware path, the SDK automatically updates any connected device whose firmware differs from the packages in that directory. This is the recommended approach for most applications.

Wait for the update to finish

Do not disconnect the device or tear down the system while a firmware update is in progress. Interrupting the update may cause the device to boot from its backup firmware, and may disable fast firmware updates on the next boot.

CC++Python 
#include <time.h>
#include <dlsdk/dlsdk.h>

dlsdk_config config = {0};
config.size = sizeof(config);
config.firmwarePath = "./DL-firmware"; // enables automatic update
config.embeddedMode = 0;

dlsdk_initialise_with_config(&config);

// Wait up to 30 seconds for the device to appear after the automatic
// firmware update completes and the device re-enumerates.
time_t deadline = time(NULL) + 30;
unsigned int count = 0;
while (time(NULL) < deadline) {
    dlsdk_get_devices(NULL, &count);
    if (count > 0) break;
    struct timespec ts = {0, 500000000L}; // 500 ms
    nanosleep(&ts, NULL);
}

dlsdk_teardown();

#include <chrono>
#include <thread>
#include <dlsdk/dlsdk.h>

// Passing a firmware path enables automatic update.
dl::sdk::Config config("./DL-firmware", /*embeddedMode=*/false);
dl::sdk::System system(config);

// Wait up to 30 seconds for the device to appear after the automatic
// firmware update completes and the device re-enumerates.
const auto deadline = std::chrono::steady_clock::now() + std::chrono::seconds(30);
while (system.getDevices().empty() && std::chrono::steady_clock::now() < deadline) {
    std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(500));
}

import time
import dlsdk

# Config() uses the firmware bundled with the package by default.
config = dlsdk.Config()
dlsdk.create_system(config)

# Wait up to 30 seconds for the device to appear after the automatic
# firmware update completes and the device re-enumerates.
timeout = time.monotonic() + 30
while not dlsdk.get_devices() and time.monotonic() < timeout:
    time.sleep(0.5)

dlsdk.delete_system()

docs.title: Manual firmware update
docs.text:
To control when the update happens, disable automatic update by initializing the system with an empty or None firmware path, then call the update function explicitly for the device.

Handles after update

After a successful update, the device and display handles remain valid, but the display must be powered on again.

CC++Python 
#include <dlsdk/dlsdk.h>

dlsdk_config config = {0};
config.size = sizeof(config);
config.firmwarePath = NULL; // disable automatic update
config.embeddedMode = 0;

dlsdk_initialise_with_config(&config);

dlsdk_device_handle devices[4];
unsigned int count = 4;
if (dlsdk_get_devices(devices, &count) == DLSDK_SUCCESS) {
  for (unsigned int i = 0; i < count; ++i) {
    // Blocks until the update completes (up to ~30 seconds).
    dlsdk_device_update_firmware(devices[i], "./DL-firmware");
  }
}

dlsdk_teardown();

#include <dlsdk/dlsdk.h>

// Passing nullptr disables automatic update.
dl::sdk::Config config(nullptr, /*embeddedMode=*/false);
dl::sdk::System system(config);

for (auto& device : system.getDevices()) {
  // Blocks until the update completes (up to ~30 seconds).
  device.updateFirmware("./DL-firmware");
}

import dlsdk

# Keep the bundled firmware path, but disable automatic update.
config = dlsdk.Config()
firmware_path = config.firmware_path
config.firmware_path = None

dlsdk.create_system(config)

for device in dlsdk.get_devices():
    # Blocks until the update completes.
    dlsdk.update_firmware(device, str(firmware_path))

dlsdk.delete_system()

docs.title: Supported architectures and distributions
docs.text:
DisplayLink Direct supports the following Linux platforms:

  • x86_64 (Intel/AMD 64-bit)
  • aarch64 (ARM 64-bit)

The SDK is compatible with most modern Linux distributions. Ensure your system meets the minimum C runtime and library requirements before installation.

docs.title: Runtime dependencies
docs.text:
The following system libraries are required to run DisplayLink Direct:

  • libusb >= 1.0.16 — for USB device communication
  • libc6 >= 2.31 — C runtime library

These libraries are typically pre-installed on most Linux distributions. If your system is missing them, install using your distribution's package manager:

Debian/UbuntuRHEL/CentOS/FedoraAlpine 
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install libusb-1.0-0 libc6

sudo yum install libusb libc

apk add libusb libc6

docs.title: Download the library
docs.text: Download the pre-built library package for your architecture from the GitHub Release Assets.

docs.title: Building with CMake
docs.text:
To integrate the SDK into your CMake project, use find_package to locate the SDK and link against the dlsdk::dlsdk target:

find_package(dlsdk 1.6.0 REQUIRED)

add_executable(my-app main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(my-app PRIVATE dlsdk::dlsdk)

Then configure and build, passing the SDK installation path via CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH:

cmake -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/path/to/dlsdk -S . -B build
cmake --build build

Replace /path/to/dlsdk with the path to your DisplayLink Direct installation.

docs.title: Disable the standard DisplayLink driver
docs.text:
If the standard DisplayLink driver (displaylink-driver) is installed on your system, it must be stopped and masked before using DisplayLink Direct, as both cannot manage the device simultaneously:

sudo systemctl stop displaylink-driver
sudo systemctl mask displaylink-driver

docs.title: USB permissions
docs.text:
By default, access to DisplayLink USB devices requires root privileges. To run applications without root, set up udev rules to grant access to users in the displaylink group:

sudo groupadd displaylink
sudo usermod -aG displaylink $USER

echo 'SUBSYSTEM=="usb", MODE="0660", GROUP="displaylink"' | sudo tee /etc/udev/rules.d/00-usb-permissions.rules
sudo udevadm control --reload-rules

Log out and log back in for group membership changes to take effect. Then you can run applications without the sudo prefix.

docs.title: Python Bindings
docs.text: The Python bindings let you integrate the DisplayLink Direct into your Python applications. Pre-built wheels (.whl) for supported Python versions and architectures are published as GitHub Release Assets.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 or higher.
  • pip available in your selected Python environment.
  • DisplayLink Direct host runtime dependencies installed on Linux:
  • libusb >= 1.0.16
  • libc6 >= 2.31

docs.title: Install from GitHub Releases
docs.text:
The wheels are published as assets on the GitHub release page. You can install DisplayLink Direct directly from a release tag without downloading the wheel manually.

Use pip's --find-links flag pointing at the release tag page (here v1.6.0). Use --no-index flag to prefer wheels from the --find-links over wheels published on PyPI. pip selects the wheel matching your Python version and architecture:

pip install --no-index --only-binary ':all:' --find-links \
    'https://github.com/syna-isd/displaylink-direct/releases/tag/v1.6.0' 'dlsdk==1.6.0'

Alternatively, install a specific wheel asset directly by URL:

pip install --no-index \
   'https://github.com/syna-isd/displaylink-direct/releases/download/1.6.0/dlsdk-1.6.0-cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_31_x86_64.whl'

Replace the Python tag (cp312) and platform tag (manylinux_2_31_x86_64) to match your interpreter and architecture.

To install the latest DisplayLink Direct wheel use: 

pip install --no-index --only-binary ':all:' --find-links  \
    'https://github.com/syna-isd/displaylink-direct/releases/latest' dlsdk

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text: DisplayLink Direct provides a compact, C-compatible API for driving DisplayLink displays without host-side drivers. Its main capabilities include:

docs.title: Driver-free, lightweight integration
docs.text:
• No host graphics drivers or compositor integration required. The SDK communicates with DisplayLink hardware directly over USB.
  • No host GPU required. Frames are encoded on the CPU and decoded by the DisplayLink device, so the SDK runs on headless servers, GPU-less single-board computers, and minimal embedded systems.
  • Embedded mode for resource-constrained systems: when enabled, the SDK does not allocate dynamic memory at runtime, making its footprint predictable and suitable for embedded deployments.

docs.title: Multi-display output
docs.text:
• Enumerate connected DisplayLink devices and their displays through a simple system → device → display hierarchy.
  • Drive multiple displays from a single host over one USB connection, with helpers to synchronize output across displays.
  • Stable hardware identifiers for devices and displays (based on the USB serial number), so the correct image is always routed to the correct output — even after unplugging or a power cycle.

docs.title: Flexible frame submission
docs.text:
• Submit frame buffers directly to a display and present them with a show / wait-on-show model.
  • Support for a range of pixel formats, including 32-bit RGB variants (XRGB, XBGR, ARGB, ABGR), packed 24-bit, and additional YUV and high-bit-depth formats.
  • Built-in frame-delta compression handled by the SDK and DisplayLink hardware.

docs.title: Display management
docs.text:
• Power displays on and off and query display size.
  • Read a display's EDID to discover its capabilities.
  • Access the DisplayPort AUX channel for advanced use cases.

docs.title: Language bindings and integrations
docs.text:
• Native C/C++ API.
  • Optional Python bindings (Python 3.10 or higher).
  • A Qt platform plugin for rendering Qt applications to DisplayLink displays.
  • Ready-to-run samples, including a video wall and an EDID reader.

Note

Swift bindings are planned for a future release and are not part of the initial release.

docs.title: Why DisplayLink Direct?
docs.text: Driving external displays traditionally relies on native video outputs (HDMI, DisplayPort, USB-C Alt Mode) and a full graphics-driver and compositor stack. That approach is limiting on systems with few or no spare video outputs, on headless or embedded hardware, and anywhere a heavyweight display stack is impractical. DisplayLink Direct addresses these challenges.

docs.title: Not enough native video outputs
docs.text: Many hosts — laptops, single-board computers, industrial PCs — expose only one or two native display connectors. DisplayLink Direct lets you drive multiple additional displays over a single USB connection, well beyond what the host's native outputs allow.

docs.title: Heavyweight driver and compositor dependencies
docs.text: A conventional DisplayLink deployment needs a host graphics driver and integration with the system compositor. DisplayLink Direct requires neither: your application submits frame buffers straight to each display through a small, C-compatible API. This removes a major integration burden and eliminates a class of driver/compositor compatibility problems.

docs.title: Embedded and resource-constrained systems
docs.text: Embedded targets often can't afford a general-purpose display stack or unpredictable memory behavior. DisplayLink Direct is lightweight and offers an embedded mode that performs no dynamic memory allocation at runtime, giving predictable, deterministic resource usage suitable for constrained and safety-conscious environments.

docs.title: Bandwidth-limited transports
docs.text: Sending raw, uncompressed pixels over general-purpose buses is expensive. DisplayLink compresses frame deltas on the host and packetizes them over USB bulk transfers to a hardware decoder in the dock or dongle, making efficient use of USB bandwidth instead of demanding a dedicated video link.

docs.title: Hosts without a GPU
docs.text: Because DisplayLink Direct encodes frames on the CPU and sends them to the device's hardware decoder, it does not depend on a host GPU. It can run on headless servers, GPU-less single-board computers, and minimal embedded systems, driving real displays from a frame buffer without any graphics accelerator.

docs.title: Direct, application-level control
docs.text: Applications that need to render and route specific content to specific outputs gain fine-grained control: enumerate devices and displays, address each output by a stable hardware identifier, submit frames in a range of pixel formats, read display EDIDs, and synchronize output across multiple displays — all from your own code.

docs.title: DisplayLink Device Requirements
docs.text: DisplayLink Direct supports DisplayLink-enabled devices that are available on the market. A representative set of products can be found on the Synaptics DisplayLink products list.

docs.title: Supported device categories
docs.text:
DisplayLink Direct can be used with DisplayLink devices across common product categories, including:

  • PCIe 3.0 extension cards.
  • USB monitors.
  • USB adapters.
  • Docking stations.

docs.title: Choosing a device
docs.text:
• Confirm that the product uses DisplayLink technology.
  • Choose a device with display outputs and maximum resolutions that match your target deployment.
  • For higher resolutions, multiple displays, or video-heavy workloads, prefer devices paired with USB 3.0 or better host connectivity.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Supported host-side operating systems and architectures for this SDK release are listed in the Supported Platforms section.
  • Actual display capabilities depend on the specific DisplayLink device, connected displays, host performance, and available USB bandwidth.
  • Device capabilities may be constrained when embedded mode is selected. See Embedded Mode for details on behavior and limits.

docs.title: Host Requirements
docs.text:
The performance of DisplayLink Direct depends on the processing power available on the host. More capable systems provide better performance, but the final experience depends strongly on the specific workload, display topology, content type, and update rate.

The following recommended specification was tested with these use cases:

  • 2 x 4K displays with a desktop workload.
  • 2 x 4K displays with single FullHD video playback.

docs.title: Recommended host specification
docs.text:
For the tested use cases above, Synaptics recommends a host with:

  • CPU: 2 GHz or faster with support for NEON, SSE2, or AVX.
  • RAM: 4 GB or more recommended for 2 or more DisplayLink displays.
  • USB: USB 3.0 port.

docs.title: Minimal host specification
docs.text:
For a basic or reduced-performance experience, the host should meet at least the following:

  • Processor: 1.2 GHz single-core CPU or higher.
  • RAM: 1 GB for 1 DisplayLink display. For 2 or more DisplayLink displays, 2 GB or more is recommended.
  • USB: USB 2.0 port.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• These requirements describe host capability only. Supported operating systems and CPU architectures for this release are listed in the Supported Platforms section.
  • Higher resolutions, multiple displays, video playback, and frequent frame updates increase CPU, memory, and USB bandwidth requirements.
